study_identification_part.si4_title: Normative modelling of brain morphometry across the lifespan with CentileBrain: algorithm benchmarking and model optimisation

study_characteristics_part.sc1_study_objective: To identify the optimal approach for normative modelling of brain morphometric data through systematic empirical benchmarking, by quantifying the accuracy of different algorithms and identifying parameters that optimised model performance.

rci9_site_effect_handling.detail: ComBat-GAM was used for site harmonization. This was compared to handling site as a random factor in the model (HBR, MFPR). The paper suggests ComBat-GAM has advantages for future applications.
rci9_site_effect_handling.supporting_text: The potential e/uniFB00ect of site on performance was addressed both by handling site as a random factor and by site-harmonisation using ComBat-GAM and then comparing the resulting models...We found no support for this assertion [HBR with site as an explanatory variable might be superior to ComBat-based site harmonisation] in our sensitivity analyses. An additional advantage of using ComBatGAM is that it removes the requirement for calibration and model parameter adaptation every time the model is applied to data from a new site.

nm2_modeling_method.supporting_text: The multivariate fractional polynomial regression (MFPR) emerged as the preferred algorithm, optimised with non-linear polynomials for age and linear e/uniFB00ects of global measures as covariates.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis: For diagnostic classification, Support Vector Classification (SVC) with AUC was used. For symptom severity prediction, ridge regression with MAE was used. Permutation tests were used to assess statistical significance.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: Normative deviation Z-scores outperformed observed morphometric measures for diagnostic classification of psychosis but not for predicting symptom severity.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed: SVC models using Z-scores to distinguish psychosis patients from controls achieved an AUC of 0.63 (p<0.001), outperforming models using observed data (AUC 0.49). However, ridge regression models using Z-scores to predict psychotic symptom severity did not perform better than chance, similar to models using observed data.

caa10_key_limitations.answer: Limited age range (few young and middle-aged adults); lack of long-term longitudinal data; generalizability to specific ancestries not tested; not all potential explanatory variables were included.
caa10_key_limitations.supporting_text: There are several methodological limitations pertinent to this study. Specifically, our study could benefit from the inclusion of more young and middle-aged adults and data from longitudinal follow-up over long periods of time. Testing the generalisability of our models to populations with specific ancestries is an important next step. We did not include an exhaustive list of potential explanatory variables.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes: The optimal models are provided in CentileBrain, a user-friendly web platform for estimating normative deviation scores.

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: The study provides a comprehensive benchmarking of eight different normative modeling algorithms and finds that Multivariate Fractional Polynomial Regression (MFPR) provides the best balance of accuracy and computational efficiency. The optimal model performance plateaued at a sample size of approximately 3000 participants.
